name: Iron Ossetian
confidence_why: Abaev 1964, the reference grammars of Akhvlediani 1963 and Bagaev 1965, Dzakhova's 2010 instrumental study of eight speakers and Thordarson 2009 all give the same rule: stress falls on the first or second syllable, the first when it holds a strong (long) vowel and the second when it holds a weak (short) one, with a shift to the first syllable marking definiteness, and they differ only on how often strong-strong words take initial stress and on a few lexical exceptions.

new_statements.quote: 1. Ударение в осетинских словах может падать только на первый или второй слог. Дальше второго слова [sic] ударение падает только в словах-заимствованиях из русского языка. 2. Если в первом слоге сильный гласный (а, е, и, о, у), a во втором слабый (ы, æ), то ударение падает на первый слог. […] Если в первом слоге слабый гласный, а во втором сильный, то ударение падает на второй слог. 3. Если в обоих первых слогах сильные гласные, то ударение падает чаще всего на первый слог. […] 4. В словах и комплексах со слабыми гласными в обоих первых слогах ударение, как правило, падает на второй слог.
new_statements.translation: 1. Stress in Ossetic words can fall only on the first or the second syllable. Beyond the second syllable stress falls only in loanwords from Russian. 2. If the first syllable has a strong vowel (a, e, i, o, u) and the second a weak one (y, æ), stress falls on the first syllable. […] If the first syllable has a weak vowel and the second a strong one, stress falls on the second syllable. 3. If both of the first two syllables have strong vowels, stress most often falls on the first syllable. […] 4. In words and complexes with weak vowels in both of the first two syllables, stress as a rule falls on the second syllable. (p. 10; p. 11 adds: 'All the rules listed above allow Ossetic stress to be characterised as bound, since it can fall only on the first or second syllable.')

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Iron Ossetian (qs-tier-2026-09-12) has an empty rule and there are no existing statements; this work supplies the placement rule (initial two-syllable window, vowel-quality/weight driven) plus mobility for definiteness and instrumental data.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is confined to a two-syllable window at the left edge and its position inside the window is decided by vowel quality: strong vowels (a, e, i, o, u; historically long) attract stress, weak vowels (y, æ; historically short) repel it. Strong-weak = initial; weak-strong = second; weak-weak = second; strong-strong = usually initial. The article calls the stress 'bound' (связанное) and 'mobile' (подвижное): it moves to the initial syllable to mark definiteness and moves onto strong-vowel preverbs. Instrumentally the stressed vowel is only 1.2x longer and 1.01x more intense than the unstressed one, but listeners located stress correctly in 205 of 218 words, so the author accepts a culminative function; there is no clear vowel reduction. Domain: Iron (literary) Ossetic.
new_statements.exceptions: Loanwords with initial stress despite strong-weak (abyræg, agwyvzæ..), strong-strong words with second-syllable stress (iron, qabaq, qatara, xabar, qazar, baba, nana, dada, mostly loans), verbs with initial stress despite weak-weak (zmælyn, mysyn, systyn, ræzyn: historical prothetic vowel, kept in Digor), oblique forms of the pronoun uyj (uymæj, uymæn, uydon) and the adverb uyrdæm, verbs with the prefix s- (sæmbælyn, sæværyn). Russian loans may be stressed beyond the second syllable. A spoken dictionary read by two normative speakers gave 108 words with divergent stress (appendix), only five of them listed exceptions; the 2002 orthographic dictionary marks stress incorrectly.
new_statements.identity_note: All three read works describe the Iron dialect / literary Ossetic explicitly (Dzakhova: 'осетинский (иронский) литературный язык'; Bagaev and Akhvlediani: the literary language based on Iron). Digor is mentioned only for contrast: Bagaev (p. 56) says Iron stress is more intense than Digor and that some authors claim Digor stress can fall beyond the second syllable; Akhvlediani/Abaev note Digor keeps the prothetic vowel (imisun, iræzun) and a definite article i.

new_statements.quote: 1. Ударение падает либо на первый, либо на второй слог от начала. […] Дальше второго слога ударение в осетинском языке может быть только в словах, заимствованных из русского языка […] 2. Место ударения на первом или на втором слоге зависит, в основном, от качества гласных, входящих в их звуковой состав: а) Когда в первом слоге сильный гласный, а во втором слабый, то ударение обычно падает на первый слог […] б) Когда в первом слоге слабый гласный, а во втором сильный, то ударение падает на второй слог […] в) Когда в первом и во втором слогах слабые гласные, то ударение падает на второй слог. […] г) Когда в первом и втором слогах сильные гласные, то ударение обычно падает на первый слог
new_statements.translation: 1. Stress falls either on the first or on the second syllable from the beginning. […] Beyond the second syllable stress in Ossetic can occur only in words borrowed from Russian […] 2. Whether stress is on the first or the second syllable depends mainly on the quality of the vowels making up those syllables: a) when the first syllable has a strong vowel and the second a weak one, stress usually falls on the first syllable […] b) when the first syllable has a weak vowel and the second a strong one, stress falls on the second syllable […] c) when both the first and the second syllable have weak vowels, stress falls on the second syllable. […] d) when both the first and the second syllable have strong vowels, stress usually falls on the first syllable. (§106, pp. 57-58; §104 p. 56 adds that Ossetic stress is expiratory with the force component dominant, and 'not especially intense, so that many people often cannot tell which syllable is pronounced with stress'; in Iron it is more intense than in Digor.)

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress lies on the first or second syllable, placed by vowel quality (strong vs weak vowel): strong-weak = first; weak-strong = second; weak-weak = second; strong-strong = usually first. Bagaev analyses apparent initial stress in words like znag, zmælyn as really second-syllable because of an unwritten initial reduced y. Further laws: suffixation of weak-vowel monosyllables moves stress to the second syllable (bæx > bæxy); a strong-vowel preverb takes the stress, a weak-vowel one does not (xæryn > báxæryn vs ærfýss); compounds carry one stress; in nouns with second-syllable stress a shift to the first syllable marks definiteness (læppú 'a boy' vs lǽppu 'the boy'); personal names are stressed on the second syllable regardless of vowels; surnames vary; a few minimal pairs (dzidzá 'meat' vs dzídza 'wet-nurse'). §107: in connected speech several words unite under one phrase stress in an accentual complex governed by the same rules.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; §106.6 (p. 60): 'Сложные слова имеют всегда одно ударение' (compound words always have a single stress).
new_statements.exceptions: Strong-weak words with second-syllable stress: abyræg, xalyvvæ, maxsymæ, agwyvzæ, basylyq (loans), Irystón, irón, izǽr, igǽr, bijyn, sijyn; strong-strong words with second-syllable stress: iron, qabaq, qatara, qadaman, qazaqag, xabar, qazar, kharu, cağar, cağajrag (mostly loans), post-1917 Russian loans (stress on 1st, 2nd or later syllable); weak-weak verbs with initial stress: mysyn, sæfyn, xælyn, ræzyn, quysyn (lost initial vowel) and prefixed s- verbs (sæmbælyn, sæværyn: contraction of sy- + initial weak vowel); pronoun forms uymæn, uymæj, uydon and adverbs uyrdæm, uyrdygæj keep initial stress (uy < strong u); kinship terms baba, dada, deda, nana and folk papa, mama stressed on the second syllable; personal names on the second syllable (Batyrbeg, Sona, Masa), shifted to the first for contempt or after kæj/cæj.
new_statements.identity_note: All three read works describe the Iron dialect / literary Ossetic explicitly (Dzakhova: 'осетинский (иронский) литературный язык'; Bagaev and Akhvlediani: the literary language based on Iron). Digor is mentioned only for contrast: Bagaev (p. 56) says Iron stress is more intense than Digor and that some authors claim Digor stress can fall beyond the second syllable; Akhvlediani/Abaev note Digor keeps the prothetic vowel (imisun, iræzun) and a definite article i.

new_statements.quote: 1. Ударение может падать на первый или второй слог от начала, притом оно больше тяготеет ко второму слогу. 2. Если в первом слоге сильный гласный (а, о, е, у, и), а во втором — слабый (æ, ы), то ударение падает на первый слог. […] 4. Если в обоих первых слогах сильные гласные, то ударение падает то на первый, то на второй слог. Притом, чаще ударяется первый […] 5. В словах и комплексах со слабыми гласными в обоих первых слогах ударение, как правило, падает на второй слог. [§10, pp.49–50] […] основной акцентологический закон современного осетинского языка сводится вкратце к следующему: ударение падает на первый слог, если он сильный, или на второй, если первый слабый. [Abaev, p.31]
new_statements.translation: 1. Stress can fall on the first or the second syllable from the beginning, and it gravitates more toward the second syllable. 2. If the first syllable has a strong vowel (a, o, e, u, i) and the second a weak one (æ, y), stress falls on the first syllable. […] [3. If the first syllable has a weak vowel and the second a strong one, stress falls on the second syllable (except the cases in points 6-9).] 4. If both of the first two syllables have strong vowels, stress falls sometimes on the first, sometimes on the second syllable; more often the first is stressed […] 5. In words and complexes with weak vowels in both of the first two syllables, stress as a rule falls on the second syllable. (§10, pp. 49-50) […] the basic accentological law of modern Ossetic comes down briefly to this: stress falls on the first syllable if it is strong, or on the second if the first is weak. (Abaev, p. 31)

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog rule is empty; this grammar gives the same weight-sensitive initial-window rule as Bagaev and Dzakhova, and adds the phrase-level accentual-complex domain and Abaev's historical derivation.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is dynamic (силовое), falls on the first or second syllable from the left edge, decided by the strong/weak vowel contrast (Abaev: strong = historically long vowels and diphthongs, weak = historically short; long vowels 'attract' stress). Strong-weak = first; weak-strong = second; weak-weak = second; strong-strong = either, more often first, especially when the first syllable is a strong-vowel preverb (a-, ba-, ra-) or the second is a formant. §9-§10 stress that not every word is stressed: syntactically bound word groups form accentual complexes under one stress, and the same rules apply to the complex as a whole (this can change meaning: činyg næ qæuy max 'we need the book' vs 'we do not need the book' by complex division). Nouns with second-syllable stress shift it to the first to mark definiteness (article function; Abaev derives this from a lost proclitic article i, still present in Digor).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; the accentual complex has a single stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Rule 7: weak-weak verbs mysyn, systyn, ræzyn with first-syllable stress (historical prothetic vowel, preserved in Digor imisun, isistun, iræzun); rule 8: personal names usually stressed on the second syllable regardless of vowels (Sozyryqo, Satana, Batyradz, Soslan, Sælimæt, Mæxæmæt, Tamaræ); numerous Russian loans need not obey the rules (kommunist, bol'shevik, patriot).
new_statements.identity_note: All three read works describe the Iron dialect / literary Ossetic explicitly (Dzakhova: 'осетинский (иронский) литературный язык'; Bagaev and Akhvlediani: the literary language based on Iron). Digor is mentioned only for contrast: Bagaev (p. 56) says Iron stress is more intense than Digor and that some authors claim Digor stress can fall beyond the second syllable; Akhvlediani/Abaev note Digor keeps the prothetic vowel (imisun, iræzun) and a definite article i.

new_statements.quote: Abaev (p. 5) makes a useful distinction between strong and weak vowels. Considering only the native Ossetian vowels (ignoring /ɛ/ and /ɨ/, since they are borrowed from Russian), he classifies /ɑ e i o u/ as strong vowels and /ə ɪ/ as weak vowels. [...] Also, whenever a weak vowel is in the first syllable of the word, the stress occurs on the second syllable, while many words with the strong vowel in the first syllable have the stress on the first syllable.¹ — fn. 1: There is a significant amount of data to suggest a hypothesis that stress in Ossetian is influenced by the information structure. In many words, even in proper names, the original stress on the second syllable shifts to the first when they are focused. [...] However, I will not attempt to analyze this phenomenon in this paper.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Iron Ossetian (src qs-tier-2026-09-12) carries an empty rule and no existing statements are listed; Hettich supplies a placement: a quality-sensitive initial two-syllable window (weak first vowel -> second syllable, strong first vowel -> mostly first syllable), following Abaev, plus a focus-conditioned retraction. Compatible with, and adds content to, the empty catalog entry; the thesis explicitly describes the Iron dialect ('Iron.. is the subject of this work', p. 2).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls within the first two syllables and is decided by vowel quality (Abaev's strong /a e i o u/ vs weak /ə ɪ/): a weak vowel in the first syllable puts stress on the second syllable; with a strong vowel in the first syllable many words are stressed on the first syllable. The author adds (fn. 1) that second-syllable stress can shift to the first syllable under focus (information structure), illustrated with ba'traz vs 'batraz, but does not analyse it further. Transcriptions throughout the thesis mark stress (e.g. [əm'bɑl] 'enemy', ['afon] 'span of time').
new_statements.exceptions: 'many words' (not all) with a strong first vowel take initial stress, i.e. the strong-vowel case is stated as a tendency; focus-driven shift of second-syllable stress to the first syllable (fn. 1, pp. 7-8), explicitly left unanalysed. Borrowed Russian vowels /ɛ ɨ/ are excluded from the strong/weak classification.
new_statements.identity_note: Hettich 2002 states that Ossetian has three dialects (Iron, Tualag, Digor) and that Iron, 'the official language of the press and television', is the subject of the thesis (p. 2; cf. p. 18 'the dialect that is described in this paper'); the author is a native of North Ossetia (BA North Ossetian State University 1997). So the statement applies to Iron Ossetian (iron1242) proper.

tone_statements.citation: Borise, Lena & David Erschler. 2022. Flexible syntax-prosody mapping of Intonational Phrases in the context of varying verb height. Phonology 39(2): 171-212. Cambridge University Press. doi:10.1017/S0952675723000015 (published online 2023; open access CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)
tone_statements.quote: To the best of our knowledge, no AM analysis of Iron Ossetic has so far been proposed. Borise & Erschler (2022) take the first step towards a systematic account by demonstrating that in neutral broad-focus declaratives, each φ in Iron Ossetic carries a complex pitch accent consisting of two tonal targets, L and H. The L portion is invariably associated with the stressed syllable in the leftmost word of a φ (the first or the second syllable, depending on vowel quality, as discussed above), and the H portion is realised on the post-tonic syllable.

tone_statements.citation: Borise, Lena & David Erschler. 2022. Mora count and the alignment of rising pitch accents in Iron Ossetic. In Proceedings of Speech Prosody 2022 (Lisbon), 871-875. ISCA. doi:10.21437/SpeechProsody.2022-177
tone_statements.quote: Our results show that (i) Iron Ossetic consistently maps nominal phrases onto φs and (ii) left φ-edges are marked with stress-aligned rising pitch accents. This confirms the observation made in the grammars that ‘stress’ in Iron Ossetic is only realized on the first word of a ‘prosodic group’. [...] The results further show that (iii) Iron Ossetic has two types of stress-aligned rising pitch accents, which we label L*+H and L+H*. In our OT analysis, we demonstrate that (iv) the anchoring of individual tones to metrical targets is determined by the moraic structure of the stressed syllable. Weak stressed vowels can only carry L*+H.

tone_statements.quote: § 9. ФОНЕТИЧЕСКОЕ УДАРЕНИЕ Ударением называется выделение одного слога в слове или группе слов при помощи усиления голоса или повышения тона. Если ударение выражается в усилении голоса, то его принято называть силовым, динамическим, или экспираторным. Такое ударение действует во многих языках, в том числе и в осетинском. [...] [p. 31:] Для древнейшего состояния индоевропейских языков было характерно тоническое ударение и независимость ударения от долготы. Однако на почве иранских языков постепенно выявилась тенденция, в силу которой тоническое ударение уступило место силовому [...]. Эта тенденция ярко проявилась в осетинском языке.
tone_statements.translation: §9. Phonetic stress. Stress is the singling out of one syllable in a word or word group by increased force of voice or by raised pitch. If stress is expressed by increased force it is called force, dynamic or expiratory stress. Such stress operates in many languages, Ossetian among them. [...] [p. 31:] The oldest stage of the Indo-European languages was characterised by tonic (pitch) accent and independence of accent from length. On Iranian soil, however, a tendency gradually emerged by which tonic accent gave way to force accent [...]. This tendency showed itself vividly in Ossetian.

readall_conflicts: No contradiction on placement: all three opened works (Akhvlediani ed. 1963 with Abaev's commentary, Bagaev 1965, Dzakhova 2010) give the same rule, stress on the first or second syllable decided by strong vs weak vowel quality, with the definiteness shift to the first syllable and second-syllable stress in personal names. Minor differences of emphasis: Akhvlediani's rule 1 says stress 'gravitates more toward the second syllable' and for two strong syllables allows either position (more often first), whereas Bagaev and Dzakhova state strong-strong = usually first; Bagaev reanalyses apparent initial stress in znag, zmælyn as second-syllable stress after an unwritten reduced y, whereas Akhvlediani/Isaev (and Dzakhova, quoting both) treat mysyn, systyn, ræzyn as historical exceptions. Dzakhova reports the stress is phonetically weak (duration ratio 1.2, intensity 1.01) and that two normative speakers disagreed on 108 dictionary words, echoing Bagaev's remark that many speakers cannot tell which syllable is stressed; she nevertheless treats stress as culminative and distinctive. Hettich 2002 could not be opened.

sources.quote: 'In Iron, where initial (unstressed) i- was lost, definiteness is marked by the shift of accent. If the initial syllable of a polysyllabic noun phrase contains a weak (short) vowel, the accent is shifted from the second to the first syllable: syrx faetk'uy myn radt "give me a red apple", but sy'rx faetk'uy myn radt "give me the red apple". If the vowel of the first syllable is strong (long) the opposition definite vs. indefinite is neutralised.' (weak = short, strong = long).

sources.quote: Abaev (p. 5) makes a useful distinction between strong and weak vowels. Considering only the native Ossetian vowels (ignoring /ɛ/ and /ɨ/, since they are borrowed from Russian), he classifies /ɑ e i o u/ as strong vowels and /ə ɪ/ as weak vowels. [...] Also, whenever a weak vowel is in the first syllable of the word, the stress occurs on the second syllable, while many words with the strong vowel in the first syllable have the stress on the first syllable.¹ — fn. 1: There is a significant amount of data to suggest a hypothesis that stress in Ossetian is influenced by the information structure. In many words, even in proper names, the original stress on the second syllable shifts to the first when they are focused. [...] However, I will not attempt to analyze this phenomenon in this paper.

sources.note: The catalog record for Iron Ossetian (src qs-tier-2026-09-12) carries an empty rule and no existing statements are listed; Hettich supplies a placement: a quality-sensitive initial two-syllable window (weak first vowel -> second syllable, strong first vowel -> mostly first syllable), following Abaev, plus a focus-conditioned retraction. sources.citation: Dzakhova, V. T. 2010. Ob osetinskom udarenii [On Ossetic stress]. Vestnik RGGU, ser. Literaturovedenie. Jazykoznanie. Kul'turologija 9(52): 9-25.
sources.quote: Instrumental study (Iron literary norm, 8 speakers + 78-listener perception test). Rules: (1) stress only on 1st or 2nd syllable; beyond the 2nd only in Russian loans; (2) strong V (a e i o u) in syll.1 + weak (y, ae) in syll.2 -> 1st, with listed lexical exceptions (abyraeg, aguyvzae, izaer, Iryston...); weak in 1 + strong in 2 -> 2nd; (3) strong in both -> 'most often' 1st, exceptions mostly loans (iron, qabaq, xabar...) ; (4) weak in both -> 'as a rule' 2nd, exceptions mysyn, raezyn etc. (historically lost prothetic vowel). Stress therefore 'bound' (svjazannoe). Definiteness shift 2nd->1st
sources.locator: 'Mesto udarenija' pp.10-11 (rules 1-4 with exception lists, summarised from Abaev, Isaev 1959, Akhvlediani 1963, Bagaev 1965); Table 1 p.13 (relative vowel durations, 8 speakers); pp.14-15 (stressed/unstressed duration ratio 1.2, intensity 1.01)

Если в первом слоге сильный гласный (а, е, и, о, у), a во втором слабый (ы, æ), то ударение падает на первый слог. sources.quote: Dynamic (expiratory) stress; phrase stress: syntactically linked word groups unite under one stress into 'accentual complexes', which can disambiguate meaning (chinyg nae qaeuy max 'we need / do not need the book'); stress in complexes obeys the same rules as in words: (1) on 1st or 2nd syllable from the beginning, 'gravitating more to the second'; (2) strong (a o e u i) in 1st + weak (ae, y) in 2nd -> 1st; (3) weak + strong -> 2nd; (4) strong + strong -> now 1st, now 2nd, more often 1st (esp. with preverbs a-, ba-, ra-, or when syll.2 is a suffix/case ending); (5) weak + weak -> as a rule 2nd

sources.quote: Instrumental (one female Iron speaker, declarative sentences): F0 and intensity, the markers of word stress in isolated disyllables, do not peak on the stressed vowel of the most prominent word in a sentence; the F0 peak is most often (52%) on the post-tonic vowel. sources.quote: To the best of our knowledge, no AM analysis of Iron Ossetic has so far been proposed. Borise & Erschler (2022) take the first step towards a systematic account by demonstrating that in neutral broad-focus declaratives, each φ in Iron Ossetic carries a complex pitch accent consisting of two tonal targets, L and H. sources.quote: Our results show that (i) Iron Ossetic consistently maps nominal phrases onto φs and (ii) left φ-edges are marked with stress-aligned rising pitch accents. This confirms the observation made in the grammars that ‘stress’ in Iron Ossetic is only realized on the first word of a ‘prosodic group’. [...] The results further show that (iii) Iron Ossetic has two types of stress-aligned rising pitch accents, which we label L*+H and L+H*. In our OT analysis, we demonstrate that (iv) the anchoring of individual tones to metrical targets is determined by the moraic structure of the stressed syllable. Weak stressed vowels can only carry L*+H.

tone.quote: § 30. Ударение в осетинском языке экспираторное (силовое). В потоке речи определяющим является не ударение отдельного слова, как в русском языке, а фразовое ударение. Группы слов, определенным образом синтаксически связанные, объединяются под одним ударением. Таким образом, значительная часть слов оказывается лишенной самостоятельного ударения.
tone.locator: §30 'Ударение', p. 560; same wording in 1952 printing p. 449
tone.translation: § 30. Stress in Ossetic is expiratory (force-based). In connected speech what is decisive is not the stress of the individual word, as in Russian, but phrasal stress. Groups of words syntactically linked in a certain way are united under one stress. Thus a considerable part of the words turn out to lack independent stress.
